title: Position: Temporal Measurement Interval Determines Computational and Model Complexity in Single-Cell Perturbation Analysis
claim: Interventions map an unobserved paired population to a later one, but only unpaired populations are observed, so matching must be inferred.
layout: 2 panels, left-to-right, dashed crossing couplings under a drug arrow
description: A left-to-right schematic of a single-cell drug perturbation. On the left, a blue rounded box labeled 'Control cells, time = 0' holds seven circles labeled x1(0) through x7(0). On the right, a crimson rounded box labeled 'Treated cells, time = t' holds seven circles labeled x_i(t), x_j(t), x_k(t), x_l(t), x_m(t), x_o(t) and x_p(t). A teal syringe labeled 'drug' sits above a thick teal arrow labeled 'transition map F_t' that runs between the two boxes. Grey dashed arrows run from each control cell to a treated cell. They cross and tangle, so the pairing looks scrambled and unknown. The eye goes first to the colored boxes and the syringe, then to the crossing dashed lines.
caption: Drug effects on individual proteins/genomes are modeled
abstract: Single-cell perturbation analysis aims to predict how cellular states change after interventions such as drug treatments or genetic edits. A central difficulty is that pre- and post-perturbation measurements are typically observed as *unpaired* populations, so accurate prediction requires inferring a latent coupling and learning a transition map. In this position paper, we argue that the *measurement time gap* is the key experimental knob controlling both the computational tractability of coupling and the effective model complexity. We identify a critical time gap $\Delta$ that induces a phase transition, under biologically inspired conditions; for "measurement-time $ \Delta$", recovering the matching is NP-hard in the worst case. The required conditions are restricted isometry of the initial states and temporal smoothness of the transition dynamics. We complement the theory with empirical evidence on synthetic and biological datasets showing a sharp regime change as the time gap increases. Furthermore, we demonstrate that a linear model can match or exceed the performance of higher-capacity neural approaches when our conditions hold.
